entry.title: Moving from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter on EKS - Field Notes from a Dev Cluster Migration

link.title: Moving from Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter on EKS - Field Notes from a Dev Cluster Migration

entry.content:
Karpenter replaces the Cluster Autoscaler (CAS) model of “grow a node group of one instance type” with “launch the cheapest instance that fits the pods that are waiting”. I tested the migration end to end on a development EKS cluster: Karpenter 1.13 installed with Helm, next to the existing EKS managed node groups and Cluster Autoscaler.

Before every step I took read-only snapshots of Helm values, EKS access entries, subnet and security group tags, IAM, SQS, EventBridge, nodes, pods, DaemonSets and PDBs, then diffed them afterwards. This post walks through those diffs and the behaviour tests.

Target design:

  • System nodes: a small managed node group, one node per AZ, fixed size, tainted node-role/system=true:NoSchedule. It runs Karpenter itself, CoreDNS, the ingress and gateway controllers, cert-manager, KEDA and metrics-server. Karpenter can’t run on nodes it manages, so these have to exist.
  • Workload nodes: a Karpenter NodePool and EC2NodeClass for every app.

Why Karpenter

  Cluster Autoscaler Karpenter
Unit of scaling Node group (ASG), fixed instance types Individual instance, chosen per launch
Capacity shortage Scale-up stalls until the ASG retries Falls back to another allowed type or AZ
Bin-packing Fixed node size Sizes nodes to the pods that are waiting
Scale-down Removes nodes when every pod can move Consolidation deletes empty nodes, and replaces under-used ones with cheaper ones
Node lifecycle Manual node group roll Drift detection, expiry, disruption budgets

The migration, step by step

1. Prerequisites: discovery tags and CRDs. We tagged every subnet and the cluster security groups with karpenter.sh/discovery=<cluster>, and installed the Karpenter CRDs.

  • The cluster already used EKS access mode API_AND_CONFIG_MAP.
  • No running workload changed.
  • A terraform plan of our cluster add-ons showed no drift.

2. Installing Karpenter. The diff here was large:

  • the controller (2 replicas, with a PDB, pinned to the system nodes);
  • a NodePool and an EC2NodeClass;
  • controller and node IAM roles, plus an instance profile;
  • an EKS access entry for the node role;
  • an SQS interruption queue and 4 EventBridge rules (spot interruption, rebalance, scheduled change, state change);
  • Cluster Autoscaler scaled to 0.

We deliberately registered the node role through an access entry, not aws-auth. Our aws-auth ConfigMap is managed by terraform, and a later apply would have removed a manually added role, leaving new nodes unable to join.

At the same step we tainted the existing managed nodes node-role/system=true:NoSchedule, to reserve them for system pods. Running pods stayed where they were. But from that moment, any new pod (a deploy, a restart, a CronJob) landed on a fresh Karpenter node. The migration begins when you taint, not when you drain.

3. Moving workloads. We replaced the managed node group with a smaller one: 5 general-purpose nodes became 3 small system nodes (one per AZ), using a rolling node group update. The old nodes were cordoned and drained, and every app pod rescheduled onto Karpenter nodes.

We then rolled the system node group once more, to a different instance type. Only the system nodes were replaced. The workload nodes and app pods weren’t touched, with zero restarts. That’s a useful property: system node maintenance no longer disturbs apps.

What broke: our DaemonSets

Right after tainting the existing nodes:

DaemonSet Desired Running Misscheduled
Datadog agent 0 5 5
Vector (logs) 0 5 5
eks-pod-identity-agent 0 5 5
aws-node, kube-proxy, ebs-csi 5 5 0

A NoSchedule taint doesn’t evict pods that are already running, so nothing went down yet. But the next rollout of those DaemonSets, or any new system node, would have come up without monitoring, logs or pod identity. At that moment every node was a system node, so a single Helm upgrade of the agent would have left the whole cluster unmonitored.

The fix for our own DaemonSets was the same toleration AWS uses on aws-node and kube-proxy:

tolerations:
  - operator: Exists

It also covers build nodes and dedicated pools added later. The pod identity agent is an EKS add-on, and its tolerations are set through the add-on’s configuration values:

aws eks update-addon --cluster-name <cluster> --addon-name eks-pod-identity-agent \
  --configuration-values '{"tolerations":[{"operator":"Exists"}]}'

Lesson: before enabling Karpenter, list every DaemonSet and check its tolerations against the taints your system and workload pools will carry.

Testing done

Environment. A dev EKS cluster (3 AZs) running about 15 small services and a few CronJobs. KEDA scales the test HTTP service on request rate.

The workload NodePool was configured as:

requirements:
  - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-family
    operator: In
    values: ["t3a"]
  - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-size
    operator: In
    values: ["medium", "large", "xlarge", "2xlarge"]
  - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
    operator: In
    values: ["on-demand"]
  - key: kubernetes.io/arch
    operator: In
    values: ["amd64"]
disruption:
  consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
  consolidateAfter: 30s
  budgets:
    - nodes: "20%"
template:
  spec:
    expireAfter: Never
limits:
  cpu: "100"
  memory: 400Gi

Method.

  • Before and after every step, a script captured read-only snapshots: EKS access entries, subnet and SG tags, IAM roles, instance profiles, SQS, EventBridge rules, aws-auth, CRDs, nodes with labels and taints, pods per node, DaemonSet coverage, PDBs, and the NodePool and EC2NodeClass specs. Each snapshot was then diffed against the previous one with diff -ru.
  • Behaviour was observed through NodeClaim events (Launched, DisruptionTerminating, DisruptionBlocked, Unconsolidatable), HPA events and the Karpenter controller logs.
# Test How Expected Result
1 Prerequisites Discovery tags on subnets and SGs, install CRDs Tags only; no workload, IAM or auth change; terraform plan clean ✅ As expected
2 Install Karpenter Helm install, NodePool, EC2NodeClass, IAM, access entry, SQS, EventBridge; scale CAS to 0 Controller Ready; nodes keep running; aws-auth untouched ✅ All created. ⚠️ Tainting the existing nodes left 3 DaemonSets with 0 desired (fixed with tolerations)
3 Migrate workloads Replace the managed node group (5 → 3 small system nodes) Apps drain onto Karpenter nodes; no stuck drains ✅ All apps moved, none unhealthy, no PDB blocks
4 Roll system nodes again Change the system node group’s instance type Only system nodes replaced ✅ Workload nodes untouched, 0 app restarts
5 Scale-out 6 pods × 1 vCPU / 1 GiB Karpenter chooses a right-sized node ✅ 1 × 2xlarge, ready in about 40s (not 5 mediums)
6 Consolidation Scale back to 1 pod × 256m Under-used nodes removed or replaced ✅ 2xlarge + medium → 1 × xlarge (Underutilized), then Can't replace with a cheaper node
7 KEDA + Karpenter Load on the HTTP service, KEDA range 1–12 Pending pods get a node fast; cleanup after the load ✅ Node launched about 3s after pods went pending; extra nodes removed 50–80s after scale-down
8 Pool limit Set limits.cpu = 5 with 4 vCPU in use, then load No new nodes; pods Pending ✅ all available instance types exceed limits for nodepool. Unrelated CronJobs blocked too. Restoring the limit launched a node at once
9 do-not-disrupt Annotate a node, then reduce load Node not consolidated ✅ DisruptionBlocked … do-not-disrupt; the other node was consolidated instead; the protected node still accepted pods
10 Remove the annotation Remove the annotation from the node Node evaluated normally again ✅ Unconsolidatable: Can't replace with a cheaper node
11 Monitoring endpoint Scrape :8080/metrics on each controller pod Karpenter metrics available ✅ 56 metric families. ⚠️ Only the leader reports the nodepools_* and nodeclaims_* series
— Disruption block window, rollback to CAS — — Not run in this round

Test details

Scale-out picks bigger nodes

Six pods requesting 1 vCPU each came up as pending. Karpenter batched them and launched one t3a.2xlarge, not five mediums. The node was ready in about 40 seconds.

Consolidation merges and replaces

When I scaled back down, Karpenter replaced a 2xlarge and a half-empty medium with a single xlarge (Underutilized). It then reached a steady state, logging Can't replace with a cheaper node. During the scale-out it had already moved the contents of two under-used mediums onto the new 2xlarge, without being asked.

KEDA plus Karpenter, end to end

Load triggered KEDA to scale pods from 1 to 12. Karpenter launched a node about 3 seconds after the pods went pending, and everything was Running in under a minute. When the load stopped, KEDA scaled back down and Karpenter removed the extra nodes within about 50–80 seconds.

Pool limits fail quietly

With the NodePool CPU limit set just above current use, new pods stayed Pending:

Failed to schedule pod, all available instance types exceed limits for nodepool
  • It blocks every app on that pool, including unrelated CronJobs, not just the one that’s scaling.
  • Restoring the limit launched a node straight away.
  • So: set limits with generous headroom (2–3× peak), and alert on nodepools_usage / nodepools_limit.

do-not-disrupt works, with a nuance

Annotating a node karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt=true produced:

DisruptionBlocked: Disruption is blocked through the "karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt" annotation

Karpenter consolidated the other node instead, and moved its pods onto the protected one. Protected nodes still accept new pods.

Observations worth planning for

  • Consolidation evicts single-replica pods freely. Ingress controllers, gateways and single-replica APIs each saw a short outage during consolidation. Give anything critical at least 2 replicas and a PDB, or protect it with do-not-disrupt, or use a disruption block window.
  • No zone spread by default. Karpenter packs nodes by cost. After consolidation, every dev app ran on one node in one AZ. Zone spread has to come from topologySpreadConstraints on each Deployment (topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone).
  • CronJobs cause node churn. With consolidateAfter: 30s, a CronJob running every 5 minutes on an otherwise idle pool launched and removed a node on every run. On quiet pools, raise consolidateAfter.
  • Set node expiry to Never before migrating. Every node created during the migration would otherwise expire on the same day 30 days later. Expiry ignores disruption budgets, and the value is fixed on each node when it’s created. Patch nodes through AMI drift instead, which respects budgets, and pin the AMI alias for production.
  • System nodes are fixed overhead. On a small dev cluster, 3 dedicated system nodes plus 1 workload node cost about 40% more than the original 5 identical nodes. The savings show up on larger clusters, where system nodes are a small share of the total.
  • Monitoring: only the leader replica reports the cluster-level metrics (nodepools_*, nodeclaims_*), so scrape each pod rather than the Service ClusterIP. Also check your autodiscovery: Karpenter’s image short name is controller, which also matches ingress-nginx’s. An endpoints-based check on the Karpenter Service avoids the collision.

Choosing instance families

Two rules from the tests:

  • Adding a family doesn’t replace anything. Existing nodes still match. A cheaper new family gets used for new nodes and gradually through consolidation. A pricier one becomes a fallback for capacity shortages.
  • Removing or replacing a family marks every non-matching node drifted, and they’re all replaced. The pace follows the disruption budget, and every pod restarts once. Add the new family first, then remove the old one in a planned window.

For a production fleet whose pod CPU requests ran about 7× actual usage, the bigger saving isn’t the instance family. It’s right-sizing requests. Karpenter packs nodes by requests, so it can’t recover CPU that’s been requested and never used.

Summary

Area Result
Enable and migrate ✅ Clean, but tainting existing nodes needs DaemonSet tolerations
Scale-out ✅ Right-sized nodes, ready in about 40s
Consolidation ✅ Merges and replaces nodes; evicts single replicas ⚠️
KEDA integration ✅ Pods to nodes in seconds, cleanup in about a minute
Pool limits ✅ Enforced, quietly. Alert on usage
do-not-disrupt ✅ Works; protected nodes still accept pods
Zone spread ⚠️ Not automatic; opt in per service

Karpenter delivered what it promised. Most of the work in migrating is in what it exposes: DaemonSet tolerations, disruption budgets for single replicas, zone spread, pool-limit alerts, and accurate pod requests.

References: Karpenter docs, Disruption, NodePools, Karpenter getting started on EKS, EKS access entries.
entry.summary: A step-by-step test of replacing Cluster Autoscaler with Karpenter on an EKS cluster. What changed at each step, what broke (DaemonSets), and what consolidation, pool limits and disruption controls actually did.

entry.title: Autoscaling on Request Rate with KEDA and Datadog - What the Docs Don’t Tell You

link.title: Autoscaling on Request Rate with KEDA and Datadog - What the Docs Don’t Tell You

entry.content:
Most teams that scale Kubernetes workloads on Datadog metrics start with the Datadog Cluster Agent’s external metrics provider. You create a DatadogMetric resource per app, then point an HPA at it. It works, but every app ends up carrying terraform for its scaling query, and the query lives far from the service it scales.

I recently evaluated KEDA as the replacement. The scaling query lives in a ScaledObject that ships with the service, in the same Helm chart or repo as its Deployment, and KEDA talks to the Datadog API directly. This post covers how a KEDA Datadog trigger actually computes replicas, a unit bug that made our test service scale straight to its maximum, and what the load tests showed.

The setup: EKS, KEDA 2.18 installed with its Helm chart, a ScaledObject per service, Karpenter for nodes, and Envoy Gateway in front of the services.

Why move off DatadogMetric + HPA?

  Datadog external metrics (HPA) KEDA datadog trigger
Where the query lives A DatadogMetric resource, applied by per-app terraform A ScaledObject in the app’s own chart, next to its Deployment
Changing a target terraform apply, then an app config change One deploy of the app chart
Link between metric and HPA Name passed through env vars; a mismatch fails silently The query is in the ScaledObject itself; KEDA creates the HPA
Other signals Datadog only 60+ scalers (SQS, CloudWatch, Kafka, Prometheus, cron, cpu, memory)
Metric unavailable HPA freezes fallback sets a safe replica count
Scale to zero No Yes

The catch: only one external metrics provider per cluster. Kubernetes routes every external.metrics.k8s.io request to whoever owns the v1beta1.external.metrics.k8s.io APIService. The Datadog Cluster Agent and KEDA both register it. To install KEDA you hand the APIService over by setting clusterAgent.metricsProvider.registerAPIService: false in the Datadog chart. From then on, any HPA still pointing at datadogmetric@... silently stops scaling. So the switch is per cluster, and every app using Datadog-metric scaling has to migrate in the same window.

What you actually deploy

KEDA scaling isn’t a field on the Deployment. It takes three kinds of resources.

1. Datadog credentials, once per cluster. A Secret plus a ClusterTriggerAuthentication. For a cluster-scoped auth, the Secret must be in KEDA’s own namespace:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: datadog-keda-credentials
  namespace: keda
stringData:
  apiKey: <DD_API_KEY>
  appKey: <DD_APP_KEY> # needs the timeseries_query scope
  datadogSite: datadoghq.com
---
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterTriggerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: datadog-keda-auth
spec:
  secretTargetRef:
    - parameter: apiKey
      name: datadog-keda-credentials
      key: apiKey
    - parameter: appKey
      name: datadog-keda-credentials
      key: appKey
    - parameter: datadogSite
      name: datadog-keda-credentials
      key: datadogSite

2. The Deployment, unchanged except for one thing: leave out replicas. Once KEDA’s HPA owns the replica count, a replicas: value in the manifest resets the count on every kubectl apply or helm upgrade. GitOps tools then show the HPA’s changes as drift. Either drop the field, or tell Argo CD to ignore it (ignoreDifferences on /spec/replicas).

3. A ScaledObject per service, shipped in the same chart as the Deployment:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: web # the Deployment to scale
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 12
  fallback:
    failureThreshold: 3
    replicas: 2
  advanced:
    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
      behavior:
        scaleDown:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
          policies:
            - type: Percent
              value: 50
              periodSeconds: 60
  triggers:
    - type: datadog
      metricType: AverageValue
      metadata:
        query: "sum:envoy.cluster.upstream_rq_completed.count{kube_namespace:my-app,envoy_cluster:httproute/my-app/*}.as_count().rollup(sum, 60)"
        queryValue: "20"
        age: "180"
        lastAvailablePointOffset: "1"
      authenticationRef:
        name: datadog-keda-auth
        kind: ClusterTriggerAuthentication

KEDA then creates and owns an HPA named keda-hpa-web. Don’t create your own HPA for the same Deployment; two HPAs fighting over one target is undefined behaviour. When you delete the ScaledObject, its HPA goes with it. The Deployment then keeps its last replica count, unless advanced.restoreToOriginalReplicaCount: true is set.

If you run a PaaS or platform layer that renders ScaledObjects from its own app manifest, it does steps 2 and 3 for you. The objects underneath are the same, so everything below still applies.

How a Datadog trigger becomes a replica count

This took more digging than it should have. KEDA doesn’t scale anything itself. It exposes your query as an external metric and creates an HPA (keda-hpa-<name>), which makes the decisions. Each decision has five steps:

  1. Query a window. On every HPA sync (every 15s), Datadog is queried for [now − age, now]. KEDA’s default age is 90s.
  2. Pick one point, without averaging. KEDA takes the newest point, or the Nth-from-last with lastAvailablePointOffset. Offset 1 skips the newest bucket, which is often still being filled.
  3. Compute replicas. With metricType: AverageValue, “average” means per pod: desired = ceil(value ÷ queryValue), clamped to min and max. Changes within 10% of the target are ignored.
  4. Limit the rate of change. scaleUp policies apply, e.g. at most +100% every 15s.
  5. Stabilize the scale-down. During the scale-down window, the HPA keeps the highest recommendation it computed.

Two things surprised me:

  • pollingInterval usually doesn’t drive scaling. With minReplicaCount ≥ 1 and no useCachedMetrics, KEDA’s own polling loop doesn’t query the trigger at all. The HPA’s 15s sync does. So each ScaledObject makes about 240 Datadog API calls per hour. With many services, use useCachedMetrics: true and watch the rate limit.
  • It’s one point, not an average. Spiky traffic means jumpy scaling unless you smooth it in the query or in the stabilization window.

The bug: .as_rate() wasn’t a rate

The first version of the trigger looked reasonable:

query: "sum:envoy.cluster.upstream_rq_completed.count{...}.as_rate()"
queryValue: "1" # 1 request/sec per pod
age: "120"
lastAvailablePointOffset: "1"

Under load, the service went straight to its maximum (12 replicas). The HPA reported about 2.1 req/s per pod across 12 pods, roughly 25 req/s in total. The Datadog UI showed the actual load peaking at about 3.4 req/s.

Querying Datadog with the same short window KEDA uses showed the cause:

.as_rate()  → 48, 51, 51, 51, 51, 49, 52, 53   (interval 15s)
.as_count() → 48, 51, 51, 51, 51, 49, 52, 53   (interval 15s)

At this granularity, .as_rate() returned exactly what .as_count() did: the raw count per 15-second bucket. KEDA got about 51 and compared it with a target of 1. In effect the target was “one request per 15 seconds per pod”, so any traffic at all maxed the service out.

The fix was to stop relying on .as_rate() and make the unit explicit:

query: "sum:envoy.cluster.upstream_rq_completed.count{...}.as_count().rollup(sum, 60)"
queryValue: "20" # requests per MINUTE per pod
age: "180" # >= 2 full 60s buckets
lastAvailablePointOffset: "1" # skip the minute still filling

Takeaway: before you trust a Datadog query in a scaler, run it with the same age window KEDA will use and look at the raw points. What a dashboard shows over an hour isn’t what a 2-minute API query returns.

Load test results

With queryValue: 20 (20 requests per minute per pod), I generated stepped load with a deliberate one-minute pause. Requests per minute come from Datadog, replicas from the HPA events.

Load (req/min) Expected ceil(÷20) HPA did
203 11 1 → 11 ✅
154 8 → 8 ✅
76 4 → 4 ✅
0 1 (min) → 1 ✅
7 (the pause) 1 11 → 1 ⚠️
  • The math matched at every step.
  • Reaction time was about 1–2 minutes to scale up and 1–1.5 minutes to scale down. That’s expected with one-minute buckets and skipping the newest point.
  • Karpenter launched nodes within seconds for pods that didn’t fit, and removed them 1.5–5 minutes after the pods left.
  • A transient Datadog API timeout raised a KEDAScalerFailed event, and KEDA recovered 8 seconds later. Fallback didn’t trigger, because it needs N failures in a row.

The pause: an aggressive scale-down plus node consolidation

The test used fast settings so it would finish quickly: a 30s scale-down window and −100% every 15s. A one-minute pause in traffic dropped the service from 11 pods to 1. At the same moment, Karpenter consolidated the node holding that last pod. The disruption budget allowed the eviction, so zero pods were available for a moment.

Two lessons:

  1. The scale-down window has to be longer than the metric’s granularity. With one-minute buckets, a 30s window means one quiet minute can remove almost everything. Use ≥180s, and keep the 300s default in production. Also cap the rate, e.g. −50% per 60s.
  2. The HPA and node disruption interact. Our default PDB for single-replica services was maxUnavailable: 1, which allows the last pod to be evicted. A PodDisruptionBudget doesn’t stop the HPA from scaling down, because removing replicas isn’t an eviction. It does stop the node autoscaler from evicting your last pod. With a single replica, though, minAvailable: 1 blocks every voluntary drain of that node, including consolidation, drift and AMI updates. The robust setup is minimum 2 replicas plus minAvailable: 1. (A follow-up PDB test is in progress.)

CPU and memory as a safety net

KEDA has built-in cpu and memory scalers, so they can sit next to the Datadog trigger in the same ScaledObject’s spec.triggers:

# ScaledObject spec.triggers
triggers:
  - type: datadog
    metricType: AverageValue
    metadata:
      query: "sum:...as_count().rollup(sum, 60)"
      queryValue: "20"
      age: "180"
      lastAvailablePointOffset: "1"
  - type: cpu
    metricType: Utilization
    metadata:
      value: "70"
  - type: memory
    metricType: Utilization
    metadata:
      value: "80"
  • The HPA uses the highest of the replica counts the three triggers ask for.
  • If Datadog is unreachable, CPU and memory keep working, since they come from metrics-server inside the cluster. Kubernetes also refuses to scale down while any metric is missing, so a Datadog outage can’t shrink the service. fallback covers the Datadog trigger itself.
  • Caveats:
    • Utilization is relative to the pod’s requests, so set them.
    • Skip the memory trigger for apps that hold on to memory (caches, JVM heaps). Otherwise they never scale back down.

Monitoring KEDA itself

The KEDA Helm chart ships with the operator’s Prometheus metrics disabled (prometheus.operator.enabled: false). Our first install ran with --enable-prometheus-metrics=false, and nothing listened on the operator’s metrics port. Without that, the useful metrics (keda_scaler_errors, keda_scaler_metrics_value, scale-loop latency) don’t exist, and the Datadog KEDA integration has nothing to scrape.

What worked even without operator metrics:

  • Kubernetes events: KEDAScalerFailed, SuccessfulRescale.
  • HPA state from kube-state-metrics.
  • Operator logs.
  • The metrics-apiserver’s :8080/metrics, which covers the adapter’s request latency and its gRPC calls to the operator.

Set prometheus.operator.enabled: true in the chart values from day one, then point the Datadog KEDA integration (openmetrics on :8080/metrics) at the operator.

Summary

  • KEDA is a cleaner home for Datadog-driven scaling than per-app DatadogMetric + HPA, but the switch is cluster-wide. Plan a coordinated cutover.
  • Enable the operator’s Prometheus metrics in the Helm chart; they’re off by default.
  • Verify the units of your query with the same short window KEDA uses. .as_rate() on a count over a 2-minute window gave me raw per-15s counts.
  • AverageValue means per pod. It’s one data point, not an average over time, and expect about 1–2 minutes of delay.
  • Make scale-down slower than your metric’s granularity, run at least 2 replicas with a PDB, and add CPU and memory triggers as a backstop.
  • Make sure you can see KEDA’s own errors before you depend on it.

Helm values we ended up with (relevant parts):

prometheus:
  operator:
    enabled: true # keda_scaler_* and keda_scaled_object_* metrics on :8080
nodeSelector:
  node-role/system: "true" # keep KEDA on the fixed system nodes
tolerations:
  - key: node-role/system
    operator: Equal
    value: "true"
    effect: NoSchedule

References: KEDA Datadog scaler, KEDA ScaledObject spec, KEDA authentication (TriggerAuthentication / ClusterTriggerAuthentication), Kubernetes HPA algorithm, HPA scaling behavior, Datadog rollup, Datadog API rate limits, KEDA Helm chart values.
entry.summary: Hands-on notes from replacing per-app Datadog external-metric HPAs with KEDA on EKS. How a Datadog trigger really turns into a replica count, a unit bug that made every service scale to max, and what the tests showed.

entry.title: CloudWatch Database Insights vs. RDS Performance Insights - A Complete Comparison

link.title: CloudWatch Database Insights vs. RDS Performance Insights - A Complete Comparison

entry.content:
CloudWatch Database Insights vs. RDS Performance Insights - A Complete Comparison

If you’re using Amazon RDS or Aurora databases, you’ve likely encountered both RDS Performance Insights and CloudWatch Database Insights. AWS is transitioning from Performance Insights to CloudWatch Database Insights, with Performance Insights being deprecated (end-of-life target: June 30, 2026).

⚠️ Important: RDS Performance Insights is being deprecated and will reach end-of-life on June 30, 2026. If you’re currently using Performance Insights, you should plan your migration to CloudWatch Database Insights well in advance.

This guide provides a comprehensive comparison to help you understand the differences, costs, and migration path. Whether you’re evaluating which monitoring solution to use, planning a migration, or trying to optimize costs, this article covers everything you need to know.

TL;DR

Quick Summary: AWS is deprecating RDS Performance Insights (end-of-life: June 30, 2026) in favor of CloudWatch Database Insights. The new service offers a free Standard tier (7-day retention) and a paid Advanced tier (~$9/vCPU/month, 15-month retention). While Advanced costs more than Performance Insights, it provides enhanced features like fleet monitoring and better CloudWatch integration.

Key Points:

  • CloudWatch Database Insights provides a free Standard tier (7-day retention, similar to PI free tier) and a paid Advanced tier (15-month retention with SQL analytics and execution plans), though some features previously free in PI (like execution plan capture for Oracle/SQL Server) now require the Advanced paid tier.
  • RDS Performance Insights is being deprecated (June 30, 2026) in favor of CloudWatch Database Insights, which offers enhanced fleet monitoring and CloudWatch integration but costs more (~$9/vCPU/month for Advanced vs ~$4.76/vCPU/month for PI paid tier).
  • Cost Breakdown:
    • DB Insights Standard: Free, ~7 days retention.
    • DB Insights Advanced: Paid, ~15 months retention, priced per vCPU-hour (~$0.0125/vCPU-hr ≈ ~$9/vCPU/mo). Example: 2 vCPU ≈ ~$18/mo per instance.
    • Performance Insights (PI) paid tier: Paid, 15-24 months retention. Historically cheaper for same retention (~$4.76/mo for 2 vCPU at 15 months), but PI console is being sunset.
  • Status: AWS is transitioning from PI to CloudWatch Database Insights. PI’s console experience and flexible retention are being deprecated (end-of-life target: June 30, 2026 per AWS comms). Expect charges to roll under CloudWatch after that date.
  • Recommendation: Use DB Insights Standard by default. Enable Advanced only for critical databases needing >7d history and advanced analysis.

Quick Start: How to Access Database Insights

Database Insights is accessible through the AWS CloudWatch console:

  1. Navigate to CloudWatch in the AWS Console
  2. In the left navigation, expand Insights and select Database Insights
  3. You’ll see all your RDS and Aurora databases that have Database Insights enabled
  4. Click on any database to view its performance metrics

Standard mode is enabled by default for new instances, so you should see your databases listed automatically. If you don’t see a database, ensure it’s a supported engine (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server) and that it was created recently (older instances may need to be updated).

Pricing

DB Insights Standard

  • Cost: $0 (Free)
  • Retention: ~7 days
  • Suitable for: Day-to-day triage, short-lived incidents, basic load analysis

📘 Reference: Amazon CloudWatch Pricing

DB Insights Advanced

  • Cost: ~$0.0125 per vCPU-hour (~$9/vCPU/mo). Example: 2 vCPU × 730 hrs × $0.0125 ≈ $18.25/mo.
  • Retention: ~15 months
  • Unlocks: Fleet views, deeper SQL/lock analysis, richer historical analysis

📘 Reference: Amazon CloudWatch Pricing

Performance Insights (Legacy Reference)

  • Free tier: Short retention (varies by engine/region)
  • Paid tier: Historically 15–24 months retention at lower cost vs DBI Advanced (e.g., ~$4.76/mo for 2 vCPU at 15 months)
  • Deprecation: Console/experience being sunset; costs may appear under CloudWatch after EOL

Note: Exact pricing varies by region and instance type; verify in AWS pricing pages and your bill.

Cost Examples (DB Insights Advanced)

Understanding the cost implications is crucial when deciding whether to use Advanced mode. Here are some practical examples:

Pricing Summary

Instance Type vCPU Count Monthly Cost (Advanced)
db.t3.micro 2 ~$18.25
db.t3.small 2 ~$18.25
db.m6g.large 2 ~$18.25
db.m6g.xlarge 4 ~$36.50
db.m6g.2xlarge 8 ~$73.00
db.r8g.2xlarge 8 ~$73.00

Note: Standard mode is free for all instance types.

Assumptions:

  • Rate: $0.0125 per vCPU-hour (provisioned instances). Month = 730 hours.
  • vCPU counts: m6g.2xlarge = 8 vCPU; r8g.2xlarge = 8 vCPU.
  • Standard mode costs $0.
  • Multi-AZ writer consists of a primary and a standby instance; some billing views count both instances. Verify in your bill whether the standby is charged for Database Insights.
  • Aurora Serverless v2: Charged per Aurora Capacity Unit (ACU) per hour instead of vCPU. Check AWS pricing for current ACU rates.

Example A: RDS setup with Multi-AZ writer (m6g.2xlarge) and Single-AZ reader (m6g.2xlarge)

Instances considered for Advanced billing:

  • Writer Multi-AZ: primary (8 vCPU) — billing only counts the active writer, not standby
  • Reader Single-AZ: 1 instance (8 vCPU)

Calculation:

  • Total vCPU = 8 + 8 = 16 vCPU
  • Monthly cost ≈ 16 vCPU × $0.0125/vCPU-hr × 730 hr = $146.00

Example B: Aurora provisioned cluster with 2 instances r8g.2xlarge (1 writer + 1 reader)

Calculation:

  • Total vCPU = 8 + 8 = 16 vCPU
  • Monthly cost ≈ 16 vCPU × $0.0125/vCPU-hr × 730 hr ≈ $146.00

Feature Comparison Matrix

Feature RDS Performance Insights Free Tier DB Insights Standard RDS Performance Insights Paid Tier DB Insights Advanced
Cost Free Free ~$4.76/mo (2 vCPU, 15-month retention) ~$9/vCPU/month (~$0.0125/vCPU-hour)
Data Retention 7 days 7 days 1-24 months (configurable) 15 months
Database Load Metrics ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes
Wait State Analysis ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes
Top SQL Statements ✓ Yes Basic ✓ Yes ✓ Enhanced with analytics
SQL Query Analytics ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes ✓ Yes
Execution Plan Capture ✓ Yes (Oracle, SQL Server) ✗ No ✓ Yes (Oracle, SQL Server) ✓ Yes (Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL)
On-Demand Analysis ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes (PostgreSQL, MySQL) ✓ Yes (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
Proactive Recommendations ✗ No ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes
Lock Diagnostics ✗ No ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes (Aurora PostgreSQL)
Fleet-Level Monitoring ✗ No ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes
Session Analysis Basic Basic ✓ Enhanced ✓ Enhanced
Historical Trend Analysis Limited (7 days) Limited (7 days) ✓ Yes (up to 24 months) ✓ Yes (15 months)
CloudWatch Application Signals Integration ✗ No ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes
OS Process Visibility ✗ No ✗ No ✗ No ✓ Yes (with Enhanced Monitoring)
Metric Granularity 1-second intervals 1-second intervals 1-second intervals 1-second intervals
Customizable Alarms ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✓ Yes

Features - Standard vs Advanced Detailed Comparison

CloudWatch Database Insights Standard Mode (Free)

Cost: $0 (included in AWS Free Tier)

Data Retention:

  • 7 days rolling history of database load metrics
  • Real-time and recent historical data only
  • Suitable for immediate troubleshooting and short-term incident analysis

Core Monitoring Features (Included):

Database Load Analysis:

  • Database load metric with time series visualization
  • Breakdown of database load by wait states/categories
  • Identify top wait events impacting database performance
  • Database time vs. CPU time comparison

Basic SQL Insights:

  • Top SQL statements by database load contribution
  • SQL query text display (limited context)
  • Basic filtering capabilities

Instance-Level Metrics:

  • Per-instance database performance drilldowns
  • Basic resource overlay (CPU utilization tied to database load)

Session Monitoring:

  • Active session count overview
  • Basic session-level insights

CloudWatch Database Insights Advanced Mode (Paid)

Cost: ~$0.0125 per vCPU-hour (≈ $9 per vCPU per month)

  • Example: 2 vCPU instance = ~$18.25/month
  • For Aurora Serverless v2: Charged per Aurora Capacity Unit (ACU) per hour
  • Pricing varies by AWS region

Data Retention:

  • 15 months of performance data history
  • Long-term trend analysis and capacity planning
  • Seasonal pattern identification

All Standard Mode Features PLUS:

Advanced SQL Query Analytics:

  • Detailed SQL performance insights with query-level metrics
  • SQL query analytics dashboard with comprehensive filtering
  • Query dimensions (database, user, client host, etc.)
  • Query parameter analysis
  • Top SQL by multiple dimensions (load, calls, latency, rows processed)
  • SQL text normalization and pattern analysis
  • Query performance trends over extended periods

Execution Plan Capture:

  • RDS for Oracle: Full execution plan capture and analysis
  • RDS for SQL Server: Execution plan visibility
  • Aurora PostgreSQL: Query execution plan support
  • Helps identify inefficient query patterns and optimization opportunities

On-Demand Analysis:

  • Available for Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL, and RDS for PostgreSQL
  • Performance bottleneck identification for selected time periods
  • Automated recommendations for performance improvements
  • Root cause analysis tools

Proactive Recommendations:

  • AI-powered alerts for impending database performance issues
  • Predictive analytics for potential availability problems
  • Performance optimization suggestions

Lock Diagnostics & Analysis:

  • Aurora PostgreSQL: Detailed lock tree visualization
  • Blocking and blocked session identification
  • Lock wait analysis
  • Deadlock detection and reporting

Fleet-Level Monitoring:

  • Monitor multiple databases from a single dashboard
  • Cross-database performance comparison
  • Sort and filter databases by load, anomalies, and recent spikes
  • Fleet-wide anomaly detection

Enhanced Correlation & Integration:

  • Integration with CloudWatch Application Signals for end-to-end application-to-database tracing
  • Correlation between database metrics, logs, and events
  • Unified observability experience within CloudWatch

Extended Historical Analysis:

  • Long-term performance trending
  • Capacity planning insights
  • Seasonal pattern recognition
  • Historical incident analysis (beyond 7 days)

OS Process-Level Visibility:

  • When Enhanced Monitoring is enabled, provides OS-level process insights
  • Correlation between database load and system-level processes

Infrastructure as Code: Terraform Configuration

Note: This section is for readers using Terraform for infrastructure management. If you’re using the AWS Console, CloudFormation, or other tools, you can enable Database Insights through those interfaces. The concepts remain the same, but the syntax will differ.

Default Behavior

CloudWatch Database Insights Standard mode is the default for RDS and Aurora instances. No Terraform configuration is required to enable Standard mode—it’s automatically enabled at no cost with 7-day retention.

Enabling Standard Mode (Explicit)

If you want to explicitly set Standard mode in Terraform:

resource "aws_db_instance" "example" {
  # ... other configurations ...

  database_insights_mode = "standard"  # Free, 7-day retention

  # ... other configurations ...
}

Enabling Advanced Mode

Important: As of the current AWS implementation, enabling Database Insights Advanced mode via Terraform still requires Performance Insights to be enabled with a retention period set. This is a current dependency that may change as AWS completes the migration.

To enable Advanced mode, you need both:

resource "aws_db_instance" "example" {
  # ... other configurations ...

  # Required: Performance Insights must be enabled for Advanced mode
  performance_insights_enabled          = true
  performance_insights_retention_period = 456  # 15 months (to match Database Insights Advanced retention)
  performance_insights_kms_key_id       = "arn:aws:kms:region:account-id:key/key-id"  # Optional but recommended

  # Enable Database Insights Advanced mode
  database_insights_mode = "advanced"  # Paid, ~$9/vCPU/month, 15-month retention

  # ... other configurations ...
}

For Aurora clusters, configure at the cluster level:

resource "aws_rds_cluster" "example" {
  # ... other configurations ...

  # Performance Insights configuration
  performance_insights_enabled          = true
  performance_insights_retention_period = 456  # 15 months (to match Database Insights Advanced retention)
  performance_insights_kms_key_id       = "arn:aws:kms:region:account-id:key/key-id"

  # Database Insights Advanced mode
  database_insights_mode = "advanced"

  # ... other configurations ...
}

Module Configuration Recommendations

  1. Add database_insights_mode variable to module configuration:

    • Add to variables.tf with default value null (which results in Standard mode by default)
    • Pass through to Aurora/RDS module resources
    • Document the parameter with cost implications

  2. Performance Insights variables (currently still required for Advanced mode):

    • Keep performance_insights_enabled variable (required for Advanced mode)
    • Keep performance_insights_kms_key_id variable (recommended for encryption)
    • Keep performance_insights_retention_period variable (should be set to 15 months/456 days for Advanced mode to match Database Insights retention)
    • Document that these are currently required when database_insights_mode = "advanced"

Migration Notes

  • Standard mode: No Performance Insights configuration needed—it’s the default
  • Advanced mode: Currently requires performance_insights_enabled = true and performance_insights_retention_period = 456 (15 months) to match Database Insights Advanced retention
  • Future changes: Monitor AWS documentation as this dependency may be removed as the migration progresses

Enabling via AWS Console

If you’re not using Terraform, you can enable Database Insights through the AWS Console:

  1. Standard Mode (Default): No action required—automatically enabled for new RDS/Aurora instances
  2. Advanced Mode:
    • Navigate to your RDS instance or Aurora cluster in the AWS Console
    • Go to the “Monitoring” tab
    • Enable “Performance Insights” (currently required for Advanced mode)
    • Set retention period to 15 months (456 days)
    • Enable “Database Insights” and select “Advanced” mode

For detailed console instructions, refer to the Getting Started with Database Insights documentation.

When to Use What: Decision Guide

Use Database Insights Standard (Free) When:

  • You need basic performance monitoring for day-to-day operations
  • 7 days of retention is sufficient for your troubleshooting needs
  • You’re monitoring development, staging, or non-critical databases
  • You want to minimize costs while still having visibility
  • You’re just getting started with database performance monitoring

Use Database Insights Advanced (Paid) When:

  • You need long-term historical analysis (beyond 7 days)
  • You’re troubleshooting complex performance issues requiring detailed SQL analytics
  • You manage multiple databases and need fleet-level monitoring
  • You require execution plan analysis for query optimization
  • You need proactive recommendations and predictive analytics
  • You’re running critical production databases that justify the cost

If You’re Currently Using Performance Insights:

  • Free tier users: Migrate to Database Insights Standard (no cost change, similar features)
  • Paid tier users: Plan migration to Database Insights Advanced before June 2026
  • Evaluate costs: Advanced tier costs more (~$9/vCPU/month vs ~$4.76/vCPU/month), but offers additional features like fleet monitoring

Migration Recommendations

  1. Start with Standard Mode: Enable CloudWatch Database Insights Standard mode for all databases. It’s free and provides 7 days of retention, which is sufficient for most day-to-day operations.

  2. Evaluate Advanced Mode: Consider enabling Advanced mode for:

    • Production databases requiring long-term historical analysis
    • Databases with complex performance issues needing detailed SQL analytics
    • Multi-database environments that benefit from fleet-level monitoring
    • Critical systems requiring proactive recommendations

  3. Plan Migration Timeline: With Performance Insights being deprecated by June 30, 2026, plan your migration well in advance to avoid service disruption. Start testing Database Insights in non-production environments first.

  4. Cost Optimization: Monitor your usage and costs. Use Standard mode for non-critical databases and Advanced mode selectively for databases that truly need extended retention and advanced features. Review your bill regularly to ensure you’re not over-provisioning Advanced mode.

  5. Test Before Migrating: If you’re currently using Performance Insights paid tier, test Database Insights Advanced in a staging environment to understand the feature differences and cost implications before migrating production databases.

References

Official AWS Documentation

  • Database Insights User Guide — Comprehensive guide on using Database Insights
  • Getting Started with Database Insights — Setup and configuration guide
  • Database Insights SQL Query Analytics — SQL query analysis features
  • Database Insights Fleet Management — Fleet-level monitoring capabilities

RDS Performance Insights (Legacy)

  • Using Performance Insights — Overview and depreciation timeline
  • Performance Insights Metrics — Metrics reference

Pricing Information

  • Amazon CloudWatch Pricing — Official pricing page (includes Database Insights section)
  • Performance Insights Pricing — Legacy PI pricing (for comparison)
  • CloudWatch Billing and Cost Management — How to analyze and optimize costs

Migration and Transition Resources

  • AWS re:Post - RDS Performance Insights to CloudWatch Database Insights migration — Community Q&A on migration
  • AWS re:Post - Transitioning from RDS Performance Insights — Transition guide article

Feature-Specific Documentation

  • CloudWatch Application Signals — Application-to-database correlation
  • Enhanced Monitoring for RDS — OS-level metrics integration
  • Aurora PostgreSQL Lock Diagnostics — Lock analysis features

Additional Resources

  • AWS Database Blog - Database Insights — Latest updates and best practices
  • AWS Support Center — Support and resources for AWS services

Conclusion

CloudWatch Database Insights represents the future of database performance monitoring on AWS. While it comes with a higher price tag for the Advanced tier compared to Performance Insights, it offers enhanced features like fleet monitoring, better CloudWatch integration, and proactive recommendations.

Key Takeaways

  1. Start with Standard Mode: The free Standard tier is enabled by default and provides 7 days of retention—sufficient for most day-to-day monitoring needs.

  2. Upgrade Selectively: Enable Advanced mode only for databases that truly need extended retention (15 months) and advanced features like SQL analytics, execution plans, and fleet monitoring.

  3. Plan Your Migration: With Performance Insights being deprecated in June 2026, begin planning your migration now. Test Database Insights in non-production environments first to understand feature differences and cost implications.

  4. Monitor Costs: Advanced mode costs approximately $9 per vCPU per month. For a typical 2 vCPU instance, that’s about $18/month. Review your usage regularly to ensure you’re not over-provisioning.

  5. Leverage Fleet Monitoring: If you manage multiple databases, Advanced mode’s fleet-level monitoring can provide significant value by allowing you to monitor and compare performance across all your databases from a single dashboard.

The transition from Performance Insights to Database Insights is inevitable. By understanding the differences, costs, and features now, you can make informed decisions and ensure a smooth migration before the June 2026 deadline.

Last updated: January 7, 2026
